note: Establish a six-column blend-recovery baseline, targeting the valuable C5/C6 fractions while avoiding difficult pure-component splits.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a volatility-ordered blend train: recover C3, C4, C5, C6 paraffin and C6 naphthene blends; then cut cost/stages and improve marginal splits. Step 1 baseline.
Six columns: root propane/isobutane; T ethane/C3; BT C4+C5/C6+; BTT C4/C5; BB C6 paraffins/naphthenes+; BBB naphthenes/C7+. Moderate 30-40 stages and R,B~2-3. Selling C3/C4/C5 and both C6 blends captures most value without expensive pure-component separations.

note: Simplify to a two-column C5-blend recovery and make both volatility splits much sharper; this directly tests whether the largest easy blend can carry the plant.
notebook:
PLAN: First prove a profitable two-column C5-blend recovery (sharp C4/C5 then C5/C6), then add only clearly paying C4/C6/heavy branches and reduce severity where possible. Step 2: C5 proof.
The initial six moderate columns were much too sloppy: every outlet was unsellable and cost $467M/yr. Largest immediate prize is C5 blend (~$613M/yr), requiring a root split between nC4/iC5 and a second split between nC5/2,2-DMB. Use substantially sharper root (60 stages, R=B=4) and B (50, R=B=3); sell all other streams. Other agents confirm moderate settings do not meet blend purity.

note: The moderate-reflux splits are far too sloppy for any blend. Test much higher internal traffic on just the two essential columns to establish whether the C5 prize can cover their cost.
notebook:
PLAN: First prove a profitable two-column C5-blend recovery (sharp C4/C5 then C5/C6), then add only clearly paying C4/C6/heavy branches and reduce severity where possible. Step 2: C5 proof.
At R=B=3-4 and 50-80 stages, the root sends ~350 mol/s C5 overhead and BT contains only ~35% C5: these are not minor purity shortfalls, so incremental stages are futile without much higher internal traffic. Test a decisive jump to root 100/R=B=12 and B 90/R=B=10. The intended root outlets are 864 and 2436 mol/s; intended BT is ~695 mol/s and >95% iC5+nC5, worth ~$613M/yr. Once split behavior is calibrated, optimize ratios/stages downward rather than adding a large tree.

note: Correct the cut positions, not just internal traffic: use low boil-up relative to reflux so the root overhead is C2-C4 and the second overhead is C5.
notebook:
PLAN: First prove a profitable two-column C5-blend recovery (sharp C4/C5 then C5/C6), then add only clearly paying C4/C6/heavy branches and reduce severity where possible. Step 2: C5 proof.
Equal reflux and boil-up were fundamentally wrong: R100's root sent 1450 mol/s overhead instead of the desired 864, and its second column similarly made a ~50% cut. For a liquid feed, the distal flow fraction is governed primarily by B/(R+B), so high R AND high B creates traffic without the required cut. Set root R=5,B=2 (about 26% overhead, matching C2-C4) and B column R=6,B=2.5 (about 29% overhead, matching C5). Reduce stages to 70 each to aid convergence and cost. The C5 target is 695 mol/s, >95% blend, about $613M/yr.

note: Drive the remaining N-butane overhead at the root while holding the already sharp C5/C6 splitter fixed; this should make the C5 blend sellable.
notebook:
PLAN: First prove a profitable two-column C5-blend recovery (sharp C4/C5 then C5/C6), then add only clearly paying C4/C6/heavy branches and reduce severity where possible. Step 2: C5 proof.
Current cut positions are now nearly right. Root at 70/5/2 gives 658 mol/s overhead and leaves about 204 mol/s N-butane in B; this contaminates BT, whose C5 blend is only 72%. B at 70/6/2.5 otherwise makes a fairly sharp C5/C6 split (only ~1% C6 in BT). Increase root boil-up from 2.0 to 2.8 to drive the missing C4 overhead; keep the second column fixed. If root recovers the C4s, its 2436 mol/s bottoms should give about 695 mol/s of >95% C5 mix in BT. Root overhead itself is not sellable without further C2/C3 removal. Avoid copying R146/R147: equal large R/B gives wrong cuts and excessive cost, and R147 failed.

PLAN: Adopt the proven three-column C4/C5 blend core, then improve profit by reducing its expensive root and simplifying light-product recovery. Step 1: secure a positive valid baseline.
My two-column C5-only attempts have either failed at the root or produced contaminated blends. R192 proves a positive 0.237 design: root cuts C5 and lighter overhead, TB splits C4 blend from C5 blend, while worthless light tops and heavy bottoms are sold without further processing. Copy it exactly before experimenting. Its root costs $261M/yr versus $467M revenue, so later trials should reduce root stages/reflux and seek modest cuts without losing convergence or blend purity.

note: Raise root boil-up to recover the large C5 loss into the worthless heavy bottoms while retaining the proven downstream blend splitter.
notebook:
PLAN: Improve the proven C4/C5 blend core first by recovering the roughly 300 mol/s of C5 currently lost to the heavy bottoms; then, if the root split is clean enough, recover the very valuable C6-paraffin blend from that bottoms stream. Step 1: raise root boil-up while retaining the converged 70-stage/4-reflux configuration.
R192 gives 0.237 with $467M revenue and a $261M root. Its bottoms contain about 300 mol/s C5, worth roughly $270M/yr, so stronger root boil-up may pay for itself. R243 shows that simply cutting stages/reflux loses C4 purity and revenue. R242's unsharpened heavy branch yields no saleable C6 blend, so do not add heavy columns until the feed split is improved.

note: Restore the cheapest proven blend core and test the large untapped heavy-branch value with two sharp splits for C5 rejection and C6-paraffin recovery.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the proven 0.238 three-column blend core, then add two sharp heavy-branch splits: first reject residual C5 overhead, then separate the high-value C6 paraffin blend from naphthenes and C7+.
Root boil-up 5.5 destroyed C4 recovery and was much worse. R285 shows 60/4/4 at the root matches 70 stages with $47M lower cost. The root bottoms still contain roughly 260 mol/s recoverable C5 plus all 970 mol/s C6 paraffins; the latter alone are worth about $1.1B/yr as a blend. Two 60-stage, reflux/boil-up 4 columns should provide clean volatility cuts if converged. Evaluate revenue and duties before optimizing their size.

note: Move the first heavy-branch cut from within C6 down to C5/C6 using low boil-up, then use a much sharper second column for the difficult C6-paraffin/naphthene separation.
notebook:
PLAN: Retain the profitable three-column C4/C5 core. Correct the heavy branch by first taking only the residual C5 overhead, then split C6 paraffins from naphthenes/C7+; optimize only if both blends sell.
The failed heavy test showed B at 60/4/4 cuts within the C6 paraffins (BT 1011 mol/s), while BB therefore cannot make a clean blend. Lowering B boil-up to 1 should move its cut down to C5/C6 and recover about 260 mol/s C5. The N-hexane/methylcyclopentane split is close, so BB needs much sharper 100-stage, reflux-6 operation. Root pressure drop 0.2 is important; 0.1 loses C5 purity. Avoid further root boil-up increases, which damaged C4 recovery.

note: Restore the proven blend core and test a thermally integrated double-effect root, targeting its dominant energy cost without changing the separation.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the profitable three-column C4/C5 core. Test whether double-effect operation can cut the root's dominant $260.6M/yr cost; if not, return to the core and improve C5/C6 recovery or make targeted cost reductions.
The heavy branch remains uneconomic: even 100 stages/reflux 6 did not make C6 paraffin blend (79%) and total reward was -0.313. Root cost dominates the profitable core. A 50/50 double effect with LP at 12 bar should give a large HP-condenser/LP-reboiler temperature gap and may save substantial energy while retaining identical separation settings. Root dp 0.2 and TB 60/4/4 are essential; lowering TB to 50/3/3 destroys both products.

note: Start from the best proven core and reduce only root reflux, preserving its boil-up and cut position while targeting the dominant condenser duty.
notebook:
PLAN: Use the improved R429 blend core (TB 3.5/3.5), then reduce the dominant root cost without losing its C5/C6 split; next test pressure or stages based on this result.
Double effect failed badly: no heat link and root cost rose to $283M, reward -0.100. R429 is best visible at 0.243, with revenue $464.2M and cost $357.8M; its TB duty reduction works. Heavy C6 recovery was uneconomic even at 100 stages/reflux 6. Raising root boil-up to 5 costs far more and destroys C4 quality. This turn lowers only root reflux to 3.5 while retaining boil-up 4, targeting condenser/energy savings with minimal cut movement.

note: Restore R480 and test a lower-pressure root, which may improve relative volatility and reduce the dominant separation cost without changing its cut.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the best R480 blend core, then optimize its dominant root via pressure and small duty/stage changes while preserving the narrow C4/C5 blend thresholds; only retain improvements.
R480 (50-stage root, 4/4, dp .2) is best at 0.244, revenue $464.3M and cost $357.3M. Root reflux 3.5 destroys C5 recovery; boil-up 5 is costly and also hurts C4. A heavy-branch column cost $134.6M and recovered nothing sellable. Double effect gave no heat integration. Current test raises root pressure drop to .3: lower pressure may improve the C5/C6 split and reduce temperature/duty costs, with diameter cost the main risk.

note: Copy R529 and reduce the side draw from 55% to 45%; its bottoms are already 100% C4, so retaining more feed should increase C4 recovery while preserving blend purity.
notebook:
PLAN: Copy the profitable R529 four-column blend core and tune its light-column side draw to recover more C4 blend without losing 95% purity; then test low-cost root simplifications only if purity holds.
R529 earns 0.304 by adding a cheap TT side-draw column ($17.6M) that recovers $43.7M C4 blend. Its TTB is 100% C4, suggesting side fraction can fall below 0.55 to retain more C4 while remaining >=95%. Current test 0.45. R480 core: root 50/4/4/.2, T 50/2.5/2.5/.1, TB 60/3.5/3.5/.1. Root changes so far hurt; heavy C6 recovery is uneconomic. Avoid broad changes and spend remaining solves on the profitable side-draw cut.

note: Reduce the unproductive light-column side draw further to retain more C4 in the already-pure saleable bottoms, while checking that the C3/C4 split remains clean.
notebook:
PLAN: Maximize profitable C4 recovery in the proven four-column blend core by reducing the otherwise worthless TT side draw; then use remaining solves for a root cost reduction if purity holds.
Current best is 0.321 at side fraction 0.45: TTB is 100% C4 and earns $53.6M, while both C3 outlets are worthless. Lowering the draw from 0.55 to 0.45 increased C4 recovery without contamination. Test 0.25 now; the side stream itself has no value, so retaining more material in the column should increase saleable TTB if the C3/C4 split remains sharp. Root reflux and pressure changes previously hurt badly; avoid repeating them. Heavy C6 recovery was uneconomic.

note: Reduce the side draw to 15%; at 25% it is already a saleable C3 blend, so drawing still less should retain more valuable C4 in TTB while keeping the C3 product on specification.
notebook:
PLAN: Maximize profitable C4 recovery in the proven four-column blend core by reducing the TT side draw; then use remaining solves for a root cost reduction if purity holds.
At side fraction 0.25 reward rose to 0.422: TTS is now a saleable 97% C3 blend ($32.6M), TTB is 95% C4 ($69.3M), and C4/C5 core revenue is $566.2M. Thus both smaller-draw predictions were right. Test 0.15: the side should remain C3-rich while more C4 reports to TTB, increasing its high-value sale. Root reflux and pressure changes previously hurt badly; avoid repeating them. Heavy C6 recovery was uneconomic. Root 40 stages saved little and slightly hurt C5 purity, so it is not a priority.

note: Adopt R671 and sharpen only its ethane/C3 splitter; the current C3 overhead still contains valuable propane and propylene, while the profitable blend core remains unchanged.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the best island plant (R671), then sharpen its inexpensive ethane/C3 splitter to recover more saleable C3 without disturbing the proven blend core; use remaining solves for targeted light-end improvements only.
At TT side fraction 0.25 reward was 0.422; 0.20 and 0.15 lost TTB C4 purity, so 0.25 is the local optimum. R671 adds a cheap 40-stage 3/3 column on TTT and sells 104 mol/s of C3 bottoms, lifting reward to 0.461. Its overhead still contains about 45 mol/s C3, so a sharper 60-stage 4/4 split may recover much of that for only a few $M/yr extra cost. Root reflux 3 caused major losses; root 40 stages and lower pressure also hurt. Heavy C6 recovery was uneconomic.

note: Adopt R717 and reduce the ethane/C3 splitter boil-up from 1.5 to 1.2, aiming to recover more saleable C3 bottoms without losing its blend purity.
notebook:
PLAN: Start from best island plant R717 (reward 0.479), tune its cheap ethane/C3 splitter for greater C3 recovery, then use remaining solves only on high-value safe adjustments.
R717 uses TTT 40 stages, reflux 3, boil-up 1.5: TTTB 131 mol/s saleable C3, overhead 50 mol/s with 37% C3. Reducing boil-up modestly to 1.2 should retain more C3 bottoms while keeping ethane below 5%; higher severity (60/4/4) reduced reward. TT side fraction 0.25 is optimal locally; root and heavy-branch changes were unprofitable.

note: Adopt the best R765 and reduce TTT boil-up to 0.8; the previous reduction recovered more C3 product and cut cost, so test the remaining safe margin.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the current best R765 and continue the successful low-boil-up trend on TTT; if improvement flattens, test a modest downstream cost reduction.
R765 (0.488) uses TTT 40/3/1.0: C3 bottoms rise to 143 mol/s and overhead falls to 39 mol/s, while ethane stays entirely out of the bottoms. Lower boil-up also reduced cost. Root and heavy-branch modifications were repeatedly unprofitable; TT side fraction 0.25 is locally optimal. Preserve the proven blend core.

note: Reduce TTT boil-up from 0.8 to 0.6, continuing the measured trend of higher C3 recovery and lower cost while checking that ethane remains excluded from the bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Continue the successful reduction of TTT boil-up while C3 recovery and cost improve; then use remaining solves for one careful downstream cost reduction.
R765 at TTT boil-up 1.0 gave 0.488; reducing to 0.8 gave 0.492, C3 bottoms 148 mol/s and cost $6.3M/yr. Test 0.6 next. Root changes, heavy-branch separations, and TB size reductions were unprofitable; preserve the blend core. TT side fraction 0.25 is locally optimal.

note: Restore the 0.492 design and bracket the C3 splitter at boil-up 0.7; 0.6 fails the 95% blend specification while 0.8 leaves recoverable C3 and duty on the table.
notebook:
PLAN: Bracket the C3 splitter optimum between boil-up 0.6 (blend fails at 94%) and 0.8 (best 0.492), then preserve the best valid design.
R765/R861 at TTT boil-up 0.8 gives reward 0.492, C3 bottoms 148 mol/s and $37.0M/yr. Boil-up 0.6 increases bottoms to 154 but ethane reaches 6%, so the entire C3 stream is lost. Test 0.7: likely retains >95% C3 while recovering some flow and cost. Root and heavy-branch changes were unprofitable; preserve blend core and TT side fraction 0.25.

note: Combine the proven 45-stage root saving with a narrowly bracketed TTT boil-up of 0.65, seeking a small recovery and energy gain while keeping the C3 blend at or above 95%.
notebook:
PLAN: Use the remaining solves for small, measured improvements to the proven blend core, then preserve the best valid design.
TTT boil-up 0.7 gives 96% C3 and reward 0.493; 0.6 fails at 94%, while 0.8 gives 0.492. Test 0.65 near the purity boundary for extra C3 recovery and lower duty. Simultaneously use 45 root stages, which preserved all stream splits in R864 and saved about $0.3M/yr. Root pressure 0.3 and TTT reflux 2.5 were costly failures; avoid further structural changes.
